strengths: The paper proposes a simple and practical critique-conditioned distillation framework that avoids multi-pass inference and preserves answer-generation format better than CFT.
The empirical evaluation covers multiple math and general reasoning benchmarks and reports gains on several tasks, especially AMC23 and OlympiadBench.
The inclusion of qualitative examples, critique-without-critique ablation, and learning-rate sensitivity analysis is useful for understanding the method.
The limitations and future-work section is honest about additional training overhead, critique quality dependence, and potential bias/fairness concerns.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is fundamentally flawed. Lemma 1's KL inequality is stated for incompatible distributions and the proof applies Jensen's inequality with the wrong direction. For convex f(x)=-log x, Jensen gives f(E[Q]) <= E[f(Q)], i.e. -log(sum_c p_c Q_c) <= sum_c p_c (-log Q_c), which implies KL(P||Q(Y|Z)) <= KL(P||Q(Y|Z,C)), the opposite of the paper's claim. Thus the claimed 'provable' entropy/KL reduction is not established.

The Bayesian interpretation in Eq. (10) is not derived and does not match the actual supervised objective, which simply minimizes -log S_theta(y_hat | x, y', c) on teacher-refined answers. Calling the teacher critique a likelihood term and the student distribution a posterior is heuristic rather than rigorous.

The empirical evidence is insufficiently reliable: no random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported. Several benchmarks are small (e.g., AMC23), so the headline gains may be noise. No repeated runs make the central empirical claims fragile.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently controlled. CFT with GPT-4o uses 50K examples, while CGD uses 100K WebInstruct examples; the teacher models differ, so teacher quality and data quantity are confounded. The paper also claims a +4.8% Group 2 gain over CFT with GPT-4o, but Table 1 shows only 36.7 vs 36.4 (+0.3) and CGD is worse on MMLU-Pro (40.3 vs 40.8) and MATH500 (54.2 vs 54.8).

The definition of 'Distilled SFT' is ambiguous/inconsistent: it is described both as soft distillation from the same teacher and as training on teacher refined answers obtained using the student's initial answer and critique, which sounds very close to CGD's target. This makes the source of CGD's gains unclear.

Reproducibility is limited: training hyperparameters, prompt templates, batch size, number of epochs, full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient tuning, decoding settings, evaluation protocol, and teacher-generation costs are not specified. No code release is mentioned. The reported 8 A100 GPU-hours appears to exclude the large-scale teacher critique/refinement generation cost.

The novelty is modest relative to prior self-refinement distillation and feedback-conditioned training work (e.g., Shridhar et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2024; Wadhwa et al. 2024). Conditioning the student on feedback and its own initial answer is not a fundamentally new idea, and the paper does not adequately distinguish CGD from these methods.

Presentation contains inconsistencies and typographical errors ('basielines', 'basedline', inconsistent LLaMA/Llama naming) and some numerical claims do not match the tables. This weakens confidence in the reported results.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and timely problem: reducing the imitation gap in SFT and the format-drift/instability issues observed in CFT-style training.

The core idea of CGD—training the student to map its own initial response plus a teacher critique to a refined answer—is simple, implementable, and conceptually plausible as a way to inject explanatory feedback during fine-tuning.

The empirical study covers several math and general reasoning benchmarks, includes comparisons to SFT, distilled SFT, and CFT, and provides an ablation on critique conditioning plus a learning-rate sensitivity check.
The authors include a limitations section and discuss the additional generation overhead and possible bias in teacher critiques.
weaknesses: There is a critical inference-time mismatch that the paper never resolves. CGD is trained to model S_theta(ŷ | x, y', c), conditioning on a student-generated initial answer y' and a teacher-generated critique c, yet the abstract and conclusion claim single-pass answer generation with no additional inference cost. If c and y' are required at test time, the method needs a teacher model and an extra initial generation pass, contradicting the efficiency claim. If they are not required, the student is trained and tested under different conditioning, so the reported gains cannot be attributed to the claimed mechanism. The manuscript does not specify the actual test-time input format or how critique is removed at inference.

The theoretical analysis is unsound. Lemma 1 uses inconsistent notation, comparing KL divergences between distributions over different random variables, and the Jensen's inequality argument appears to yield the opposite inequality direction. Conditioning on an arbitrary critique does not generally reduce KL divergence to a target distribution; a bad or misleading critique can increase it. The Bayesian interpretation in Eq. (10) is an informal analogy rather than a derivation of the training objective, and the abstract's claim of an entropy-based analysis is not backed by any entropy measurement in the experiments.

The empirical evidence is not strong enough to support the central claims. The AMC23 result (e.g., 22.5 to 37.5) is a very large gain on a small benchmark, reported without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and WebInstruct is web-crawled data that may overlap with AMC-style problems. No decontamination analysis is provided, making the headline math gains questionable.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently apples-to-apples. CFT* with GPT-4o uses a stronger teacher and a different 50K WebInstructCFT subset in key comparisons, while CGD uses LLaMA3.3-70B and 100K WebInstruct samples. The Distilled SFT baseline is also ambiguously specified: it is said to use teacher refined answers generated with the critique, but it is unclear whether the student sees the same inputs as CGD. In Table 3, the Group 2 average gain over CFT is only 33.5 vs. 33.4, yet the text claims CGD outperforms all baselines.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper reports no training hyperparameters, prompt templates, evaluation or answer-extraction protocol, full fine-tuning versus parameter-efficient setup, random seeds, or error bars. The compute description ('16 Nvidia A100 GPUs for 30 minutes, 8 A100 GPU-hours per experiment') is suspiciously low for full fine-tuning an 8B model on 100K samples and is not explained. No code, data, or model artifacts are released.

The format-drift and efficiency claims are only partially supported. The format-drift mitigation is illustrated with one qualitative example, and the IFEval comparison uses only the GPT-4o CFT baseline for the most striking degradation. Figure 5's 'CGD without critique' still uses an initial response y', which implies an extra generation pass and again conflicts with the claim of no added inference cost.

The presentation has many typographical and consistency issues (e.g., 'basielines', shifting numbers between abstract and tables, unclear baseline definitions), and the paper does not clearly distinguish its method from a privileged-information distillation approach. Without clarifying the inference-time conditioning, the main contribution and its claimed efficiency advantage are not established.

strengths: The paper targets a real limitation of SFT and CFT: naive critique fine-tuning can cause format drift, and multi-pass critique/refinement is expensive at inference. The proposed CGD is simple and could be useful if its inference-time protocol were clearly specified and fair.

The empirical evaluation spans multiple math and general reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, Minerva-Math, GSM8K, OlympiadBench, AMC23, TheoremQA, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, MUSR, TruthfulQA, BBH) and two training datasets, which gives a broad initial view of the method's behavior.
The paper includes an ablation on critique conditioning and a learning-rate sensitivity comparison against CFT, showing that CGD is more robust than CFT at higher learning rates.
The qualitative examples illustrate the intended distinction from CFT: CFT may drift toward critique-style outputs, while CGD can produce a refined answer in the original answer format.
The limitations section acknowledges computational overhead, dependence on critique quality, and fairness/safety considerations, which is appropriate, though limited in depth.
weaknesses: The central theoretical analysis is not sound. Lemma 1 is not well-posed: it compares KL divergences between distributions over different random variables (e.g., KL(P(X)||Q(Y|Z))), and the proof incorrectly applies Jensen's inequality. In fact, for a mixture over critiques, -log is convex, so the marginal KL is generally less than or equal to the conditional KL, not greater than or equal to it, reversing the claimed inequality. Consequently, Eq. (9) and the claimed optimization benefit are not established.

The Bayesian interpretation in Eq. (10) is not derived from the training objective. The teacher critique c is generated from (x, y'), not from the refined answer yhat, so T_phi(c | x, y', yhat) is not the likelihood actually used. The posterior/likelihood analogy is therefore informal and does not support the uncertainty-reduction claim.

The inference protocol is critically unclear. CGD trains the student to condition on x, the initial response y', and the teacher critique c. At deployment, y' and especially c are not generally available without either a separate initial-generation pass and teacher/self-critique pass or a train-test mismatch. The paper does not specify how evaluation prompts are constructed, and this directly affects the claimed 'no additional inference-time cost' and single-pass deployment advantage.

The baselines are not fully apples-to-apples. CFT* with GPT-4o uses a different teacher and only 50K examples, while CGD is compared mainly to a weaker LLaMA-3.3-70B CFT. Against GPT-4o CFT, CGD's Group 2 average gain is only +0.3, and it is lower on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. The abstract highlights favorable AMC23 gains without adequately contextualizing mixed results.

There is no statistical significance testing or variance reporting. Several benchmarks (e.g., AMC23) have few examples, and large reported differences such as +15.0 over CFT on AMC23 may be within noise. Multiple seeds or confidence intervals are needed to support the main empirical claims.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The paper omits essential training details (learning rates, batch sizes, sequence lengths, decoding settings, prompt templates for teacher critique/refinement, evaluation parsing, number of samples), and it does not provide code or data generation scripts. The 30-minute/8-A100-hour training setup is also not described precisely enough to reproduce.

The paper does not analyze training-test contamination. WebInstruct and MetaMathQA may contain problems overlapping with MATH500, AMC23, OlympiadBench, etc., and no contamination check or held-out construction is reported. This is especially important given large math gains.

Evaluation is limited to one student model (Llama-3.1-8B Instruct). The paper argues that CFT works better for stronger reasoners such as Qwen-2.5, but does not test CGD on such models, leaving generalizability unknown.

The format-drift claim is demonstrated only qualitatively; there is no quantitative measure of format drift, and the IFEval drop for CFT may partly reflect the GPT-4o teacher/data rather than CFT itself. The comparison is therefore not decisive.

Novelty is incremental relative to prior distillation/self-refinement work (e.g., Shridhar et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2024): the core change is to condition the student on a teacher critique and initial answer while supervising the refined answer. The related-work section does not fully clarify how CGD differs from those feedback-distillation pipelines beyond choosing the refined answer as the training target.

strengths: Proposes Critique-Guided Distillation (CGD), a multi-stage fine-tuning framework that trains a student on (prompt, initial answer, teacher critique) -> refined teacher answer, with the goal of learning self-correction without deploying critique/revision passes at inference.

Experiments span LLaMA and Qwen/S1.1 families, multiple student/teacher scales, math/general reasoning benchmarks, instruction-following, factual accuracy, and include several ablations (teacher choice, dataset, learning rate, critique mixture).

Reports substantial gains over SFT, Distilled SFT, and CFT on some benchmarks (e.g., +15.0 on AMC23, +12.2 on MATH-500 for S1.1-3B over CFT in Table 1) and qualitatively illustrates CFT's format drift.
Provides diagnostic attempts (entropy, gradient norm, attention, counterfactual case study) and acknowledges limitations and future work.
Reproducibility is partially supported by code/instructions in an appendix and explicit hyperparameters for the main experiments.
weaknesses: The central methodology has a serious train-test mismatch: during training the model is conditioned on the student's initial answer and the teacher critique, but at inference the paper claims only the prompt is provided. The manuscript does not explain how the prompt is formatted at test time, whether critique is removed or masked, or why a model trained on this conditional distribution should match prompt-only inference. This undermines the claimed mechanism and single-pass equivalence.

Experimental details and compute comparisons are inconsistent: Table 3 reports CGD scores (e.g., MATH500 29.4) that are far lower than Table 1 CGD scores (54.2) on LLaMA3.1-8B, and the base-vs-Instruct setting for the SimpleRL-Zero comparison is unclear. The compute claim '60x less compute' is not consistently supported (setup says 8 A100 GPU-hours per experiment, later comparison says 8x A100 for ~5 hours, while SimpleRL-Zero is 32 H100s for 1.5 days).

Statistical rigor is insufficient: no confidence intervals or standard deviations appear in the main tables despite claims of three random seeds. Benchmarks like AMC23 and OlympiadBench have small test sets, so large absolute gains (e.g., +15.0) may be noisy and are not shown with significance tests.

Baseline comparisons are potentially unfair or selectively reported: CFT* with GPT-4o uses 50K samples while CGD uses 100K and a different teacher; Table 2 argues critique fine-tuning degrades general capabilities using only CFT* with GPT-4o, omitting the same-teacher CFT baseline from that table. The cost of generating 100K critiques with a 70B teacher is not included in the efficiency comparisons.

The diagnostic evidence is weak and sometimes overinterpreted: mean entropy differences are tiny (6.56 vs 6.44), lower gradient norm does not necessarily indicate more efficient learning, attention patterns are descriptive rather than causal, and the counterfactual robustness test is a single-sample case study explicitly not run at scale.

The Bayesian interpretation is superficial and not formally tied to the training objective; it presents a proportionality involving an unnormalized teacher likelihood without theoretical development, and the practical implementation is standard supervised fine-tuning on augmented context.

Novelty is limited relative to prior critique-based and self-correction distillation work; CGD largely combines existing ideas (teacher critiques, refined answers, supervised fine-tuning) with an additional context-conditioned training objective, but lacks formal justification for why this should generalize to prompt-only inference.

The paper overclaims, describing CGD as a 'state-of-the-art', 'robust and generalizable alternative to both conventional SFT and RL-based methods' despite limited baselines, no benchmark contamination analysis, and no error bars; limitations discussion does not sufficiently address the inference-time mismatch.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reducing inference-time cost of critique/refinement while improving reasoning.
Presents an extensive empirical suite across LLaMA, Qwen/S1.1, Mixtral, and OLMo, with several ablations and diagnostic probes.
Reports several notable gains over SFT/CFT on hard math benchmarks, especially AMC23 and OlympiadBench for LLaMA3.1-8B Instruct.
Has a clear high-level pipeline and includes a limitations section that acknowledges dependence on student receptivity and data-generation cost.
weaknesses: Fundamental train-test mismatch: CGD is trained as S_theta(hat y | x, y', c), but at inference it supposedly uses only x. Since y' and c are generated from privileged information and the target hat y is conditioned on them, the objective does not train the required x -> hat y mapping. No context-distillation KL/context-dropout objective is described. This undermines the central claim that CGD learns a single-pass prompt-only policy.

Compute/efficiency claims are inconsistent and unsupported: main experiments claim 16 A100 GPUs for 30 min (8 A100-hours) for 100K examples and 8B full fine-tuning, which is implausibly small; the RL comparison uses a different estimate (8 A100 GPUs for ~5 h); the abstract claims 60x less compute than SimpleRL-Zero, but the supplied numbers imply roughly an order of magnitude at best, and teacher-generation cost for 100K critiques/refinements is excluded.

The SimpleRL-Zero comparison in Table 3 is not apples-to-apples: CGD there is reported on LLaMA3.1-8B base (MATH500 29.4, avg 11.9), far below the LLaMA3.1-8B Instruct results in Table 1 (MATH500 54.2, avg 46.9). The abstract's claim that CGD 'approaches or exceeds' SimpleRL-Zero is therefore misleading unless one specifies the base-model setting; it also underperforms SimpleRL-Zero on AMC23 (10.0 vs 15.0).

Main results lack statistical rigor: no error bars or confidence intervals are reported despite the paper saying results are averaged over three seeds. Benchmarks such as AMC23 and OlympiadBench are small, so gains like +15.0 and +12.2 may be within noise. No significance tests are provided for the main claims.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing or fair. CFT* with GPT-4o uses 50K different samples/teacher, CFT is reimplemented without enough detail, and the claimed format-drift failure of CFT may be a strawman depending on how CFT is evaluated. The paper also omits comparisons to context distillation, rationale distillation, rejection sampling, and other recent reasoning fine-tuning methods, so 'state-of-the-art' is unsupported.

Novelty is limited relative to prior critique/self-refinement and context-distillation work. The method is basically supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated refined answers while including extra context during training; the only real difference from the Distilled SFT baseline is the presence of y' and c at training time, which is precisely the setting that creates the train-test mismatch.

The Bayesian interpretation in Eq. 2 is post hoc and technically incorrect as written: the training objective is NLL against a point target, not KL to the teacher posterior, and the equation is a proportionality with an unnormalized 'likelihood'. It does not explain or justify the algorithm.

Reproducibility is inadequate: teacher prompting templates, critique filtering/selection, data splits, random seeds, evaluation prompts, and exact-match extraction are not sufficiently specified. Code is only promised in supplementary material, and the reported training compute inconsistency further prevents reliable reproduction.

Diagnostic evidence is overinterpreted: lower entropy is treated as better even though it may reflect miscalibration; gradient-norm reduction may simply follow from lower loss; attention visualizations are descriptive without causal tests; and the counterfactual robustness claim rests on a single qualitative sample (n=1) by the authors' own admission.

Generalization is not as consistent as claimed: on MetaMathQA, CGD gains only +0.1 average over CFT on Group 2 and loses on Minerva-Math/GSM8K; Mixtral CGD loses on AMC23 and GPQA; OLMo gains are small; Table 2 shows BBH lower than the base model. This contradicts the 'consistently improves' narrative.

strengths: The proposed CGD idea is intuitive: during training, condition on the student's own flawed answer and a teacher critique, and supervise the refined teacher answer; this could in principle combine the benefits of critique-based and answer-based distillation while avoiding multi-pass inference.

The empirical study is broad, covering two model families, two training datasets, multiple math and general reasoning benchmarks, several student/teacher configurations, ablation studies, and a comparison against an RL-based baseline.
The paper motivates an important practical problem: conventional SFT and critique fine-tuning can be brittle, and inference-time critique/refinement methods are expensive.
The paper includes a limitations section, hyperparameter details, and supplementary code, which is a useful starting point for reproducibility.
Several ablations, such as removing the critique and varying learning rates, provide evidence that the critique and refined-answer supervision contribute to the reported gains.
weaknesses: The central train-test claim is not adequately supported: the training objective is S_theta(y_hat | x, y', c), but at inference the model is presented with only x and expected to output the refined answer. No training procedure for this prompt-only condition is described (e.g., dropping y', c, training a prompt-only branch, or having the model generate an internal critique). This is a fundamental mismatch that undermines the claimed single-pass, no-critique inference method.

The main baselines and comparisons are confounded. CGD uses additional conditioning on y' and c relative to Distilled SFT, and at test time it is not trained to imitate the refined answer from x alone. The gains may therefore reflect extra conditioning or regularization rather than genuine internalization of critique-guided reasoning.

The efficiency claims are not credible as stated. The compute accounting for teacher data generation is omitted, and GPU-hour numbers are inconsistent across the paper (e.g., 16 A100 GPUs for 30 minutes equals 8 GPU-hours, later 8 A100 GPUs for ~5 hours, while the RL comparison uses 32 H100 GPUs for 1.5 days). The 60x compute reduction claim ignores the cost of generating 100K teacher critiques and refined responses with a 70B teacher.

Evaluation robustness is limited. There are no confidence intervals or error bars for the main benchmark gains; several large improvements are concentrated on small benchmarks such as AMC23 and OlympiadBench. Exact-match parsing is not fully specified, and possible train-test contamination is not checked (e.g., MetaMathQA is derived from GSM8K/MATH while evaluation uses MATH500/GSM8K; WebInstruct is web-crawled and may overlap with evaluation sets).

The comparison to CFT on general capabilities is incomplete: Table 2 evaluates only CFT* with GPT-4o and not their own CFT trained with LLaMA3.3-70B, so the claim that CFT broadly degrades instruction following is weaker than presented. The CFT* comparison also uses 50K samples versus 100K for CGD, confounding data quantity with method.

The diagnostic evidence is thin. The entropy differences are tiny (e.g., 6.44 vs 6.49) despite significance markers, attention analyses use only 50 samples, the counterfactual case study is an anecdote, and the Bayesian posterior interpretation is formal and superficial rather than derived or tested.

The paper is not reproducibly presented. It lacks prompt templates, exact critique/refinement generation prompts, parsing procedures, seed-level variance, and clear training-time input formatting. The absence of these details makes it difficult to determine how prompt-only inference is actually performed.

The presentation quality is poor: the references contain numerous errors, placeholders, duplicated or garbled citations, and typos such as “G5M8K,” “GLMo,” and misspelled author names. This is not just cosmetic; it reduces confidence in the rigor of the work.

The originality and significance are incremental over prior critique/refinement and feedback distillation work. The paper does not compare against several directly relevant prior methods that train students to use feedback/refinement, and the abstract/conclusion make safety and robustness claims that are not empirically evaluated.
